How structured settlement buyouts work

A structured settlement buyout lets you sell some or all of your future payments for a lump sum today. Buyers apply a discount rate, typically 9% to 18% a year, and a judge must approve every sale before money changes hands.

By Amina Benali · Updated recently

What does a buyout cost?

The cost is the gap between what your payments are worth and what you receive. On $100,000 paid over 10 years, a 12% discount rate returns about $56,500 today, while a 9% rate returns about $64,200. That $7,700 difference is why comparing at least three quotes matters.

Discount rateLump sum on $100,000 over 10 years
9%$64,200
12%$56,500
18%$44,900

How long does a buyout take?

Most sales close in 45 to 90 days. Federal law (26 U.S.C. § 5891) requires court approval, and 49 states have protection acts that add a hearing. You can read the statute at Cornell Law and state rules at NCSL, and consumer guidance from the CFPB and FTC.

Is selling my payments a good idea?

It can be, when the cash prevents a costlier problem, such as foreclosure or 29% credit card interest. It rarely makes sense for discretionary spending.

"Most people who regret a sale took the first offer without comparing," says Daniel Ortiz, a settlement planner with 20 years of experience.
  • Get at least three written quotes.
  • Ask for the effective discount rate, not just the lump sum.
  • Sell only the payments you need to.
  • Ask whether fees are included in the quote.

Which payments can you sell?

You can sell all future payments, a fixed number of them, or a portion of each one. Partial sales let you keep income for later years while still covering an urgent cost today. Life-contingent payments, which stop if you die, sell at deeper discounts of about 2 to 4 percentage points because buyers price in mortality risk.

Annuity companies such as MetLife and Prudential issue most structured settlement annuities. The company keeps paying as before; the court order simply redirects the payments you sold to the buyer. Your remaining payments, if any, continue to come to you on the original schedule.

What should you ask a buyer?

Ask for the effective annual discount rate, every fee in writing, the expected hearing date, and whether you can cancel before the hearing. Reputable buyers answer all four in their first written quote, usually within 24 hours. A buyer who won't state the rate is hiding the most important number in the deal.

Also ask who pays for independent professional advice. Many states require you to get it, and in 21 states the buyer must pay for it. That review often catches quotes that are 10% to 15% below market.
